title: Meet a neuron in 3D.
intro: Before a neuron sends a signal, it holds a quiet electrical difference across its membrane.
In this model, that resting potential is −65 millivolts; without an input, the voltage stays there.
Rotate the schematic neuron to see its branching inputs, cell body, and myelinated axon.

symbols.meaning: The membrane’s current electrical potential, in mV.
The resting level: −65 mV in this teaching model.

terms.definition: The boundary that holds the voltage difference.
The branching input tree. The slider applies one lumped input current to the model, not a separate current in each branch.
The output path that carries the neuron’s signal away from its cell body.
Insulating sheaths illustrated around the axon. Their geometry does not change this single-compartment calculation.

predict.question: With no input, what happens to a neuron at rest?
predict.why: At rest with I = 0, both the input and the voltage difference from rest are zero. There is no net change, so the model remains at −65 mV.

challenge.text: Set input to 0 nA and watch the voltage and spike count.

figure_caption: A schematic neuron in three dimensions. Rotate it to inspect dendrites, soma, and the myelinated axon.

source.title: One neuron in three dimensions: demonstration notes

learning.objective: Understand why zero input leaves the voltage at rest.
learning.action: Set input to 0 nA and watch the voltage and spike count.
learning.observe: The membrane stays at −65 mV and the spike count stays zero.
learning.mechanism: At rest, input and leak cancel to zero, so the voltage derivative is zero.

title: Input arrives at the dendrites.
intro: Input collects in the branching dendrites and flows into the cell body, the soma.
In the soma the input charges the membrane while a leak pulls it back toward rest; the time constant sets how fast it settles.

symbols.meaning: Input current, in nA; the resistance R is fixed at 10 MΩ.
Time constant, in ms: a larger value means a slower response.

terms.definition: The branching input tree. The slider applies one lumped input current to the model, not a separate current in each branch.
The cell body. Its single membrane voltage stands for the whole neuron in this model.
The tendency for the membrane voltage to move back toward rest.

predict.question: You set the input to 1 nA. Where does the soma’s voltage settle?
options: At −55 mV, below the trigger level.
It keeps rising without a limit.
predict.why: With R = 10 MΩ the voltage settles at Vrest + RI = −65 + 10 = −55 mV. There the leak exactly balances the input, so it stays below the −50 mV threshold.

challenge.text: Set input to 1 nA and watch voltage approach its subthreshold equilibrium.

figure_caption: Input particles flow along the dendrites into the soma. One voltage represents the whole cell; the anatomy is illustrative, not a cable model.

source.title: One neuron in three dimensions: demonstration notes

learning.objective: See input and leak compete, and τ control response speed.
learning.action: Set input to 1 nA and watch voltage approach its subthreshold equilibrium.
learning.observe: Voltage rises toward −55 mV without reaching the −50 mV threshold.
learning.mechanism: RI=10 mV balances the membrane leak when the voltage is 10 mV above rest.

title: The trigger zone decides.
intro: Where the axon leaves the soma, the trigger zone watches the membrane voltage.
When it reaches −50 mV the model emits a spike, resets to −65 mV and holds there for 2 ms.

symbols.meaning: Firing threshold, in mV: cross it to emit a spike.
Reset voltage, in mV, held during the 2 ms refractory interval.

terms.definition: The axon hillock, drawn where the axon begins. The model fires when the voltage reaches −50 mV.
A discrete output event: a pulse leaves the trigger zone and travels along the axon.
After a spike, voltage returns to −65 mV before integration resumes.

predict.question: At 1.4 nA, does a pulse ever leave the trigger zone?
options: No. The voltage settles at −51 mV, just below threshold.
Yes, once enough charge builds up.
predict.why: At 1.4 nA the voltage settles at −65 + 14 = −51 mV and never reaches −50 mV. In this model the input must exceed 1.5 nA to fire.

challenge.text: Set input to 2 nA and observe the reset events in the voltage trace.

figure_caption: Each calculated spike leaves the trigger zone as a pulse along the axon. Transit is slowed for illustration, not a measured conduction speed.

source.title: One neuron in three dimensions: demonstration notes

learning.objective: Connect the threshold crossing to a discrete output spike.
learning.action: Set input to 2 nA and observe the reset events in the voltage trace.
learning.observe: Voltage ramps to −50 mV, then resets; spikes accumulate in the first-second count.
learning.mechanism: After each threshold crossing, the model resets to −65 mV and holds for 2 ms.

title: Follow the signal down the axon.
intro: Stronger input shortens the climb to threshold, so pulses leave the trigger zone more often.
Our simulation produced 33 spikes at 2 nA and 63 at 3 nA in the first 1 s (0–1000 ms); the axon and terminal tags count the same window.

symbols.meaning: Firing rate in Hz, shown at the axon terminals.
Spikes counted in the first 1 s (0–1000 ms), shown on the axon.
Input current in nA; R = 10 MΩ.

terms.definition: Where pulses arrive. The tag shows the firing rate from the first 1 s.
Time between two spikes; shorter intervals mean a faster rhythm.
Insulating sheaths illustrated around the axon. Their geometry does not change this single-compartment calculation.

predict.question: Real myelin speeds up signals. Does it change the spike count in this model?
options: No. This model has one voltage, so myelin is illustration only.
Yes. More myelin means more spikes.
predict.why: This single-compartment model has one membrane voltage and no cable, so myelin and branch length cannot change the count. Our simulation gives 33 spikes at 2 nA and 63 at 3 nA in the first 1 s (0–1000 ms), matching the checked Python reference.

challenge.text: Set input to 3 nA and wait for the first 1,000 ms measurement.

figure_caption: Stronger current produces more calculated spikes; each one travels to the terminals. Counts cover the first 1 s of the run.

source.title: One neuron in three dimensions: demonstration notes

learning.objective: Compare rates using the same measurement window.
learning.action: Set input to 3 nA and wait for the first 1,000 ms measurement.
learning.observe: The first-second count is 63 spikes, compared with 33 at 2 nA.
learning.mechanism: A stronger input shortens the time to threshold after each reset.
